<p>ENGINE VEHICLE INTERFACE (AP 71-016) Figure 15. 
</p>
<p>Theprimary interface between the engine und the vehicle is the structural 
</p>
<p>attachments and the propellant feed ducts, The secondary interface is the 
</p>
<p>flow of propellant tank pressurant and.control signals and actuation power. 
</p>
<p>Since the engine system is not gimbaled 1 many designrequirements usually 
</p>
<p>associated with an engine vehicle int~rface have been eliminated, i.e., the 
</p>
<p>great variety of flexible and/or gimbaling lines is not required. Also, 
</p>
<p>location restrictions imposed by gimbaling requirements as to where the 
</p>
<p>lines may be routed have been eliminated. 
</p>
<p>The structural interface is the conical thrust structure attachment to 
</p>
<p>the vehicle and the base injection section attachme.nt to the structure. 
</p>
<p>The thrust structure is attached using two bolts at each axial beam 
</p>
<p>location (144 beams located 2° 30' apart}, The base injection section 
</p>
<p>is attached by a simple supported seal. 
</p>
<p>The propellant feed ducts must have enough flexibility to allow for 
</p>
<p>installation alignment and th~rmal changes brought about by th~ propellants, 
</p>

<p>SERV TlffiUS'f CIIAM13ER COOLING ANALYSIS 
</p>
<p>The SERV engine consists of an annular combustor expansing hot combustion 
</p>
<p>gases on a truncated aerospike nozzle. The combustor, Fig,16 , is about 
</p>
<p>5 inches in length from the injector face to throat plane with a throat 
</p>
<p>gap (neglecting baffles) of 0,5806 inches and injector end height of 
</p>
<p>1.5 inches. The combustor aiis is canted radially outward 62,3 degrees 
</p>
<p>with respect to the engine centerbody axis· of symmetry. The combustor 
</p>
<p>shroud extends about 4,8 inches below the throat to an area ratio of 
</p>
<p>about 5,5. 
</p>
<p>The combustor including the shroud will be fabricated from_a NARloy casting 
</p>
<p>or billet with coolant passages machined on the outer contour. The coolant 
</p>
<p>passages are closed out with an slecrodeposited nickel backwall ~hich also 
</p>
<p>provides structural rigidity for the contour, 
</p>
<p>Coolant passages for the combustor throat should be about 0.050 inches 
</p>
<p>square with a 0.060 inch land. The gas-side wall thickness for the 
</p>
<p>expected heat flux at 2000 P is about 0.035 inches, which should also 
C 
</p>
<p>meet other requirements. If constant land thickness is maintained 
</p>
<p>throughout the combustor length, passage width will be about 0.052 inches 
</p>
<p>at the injector and about 0,051 at the shroud exit, An engine combustor 
</p>
<p>segment will contain about 100 passages. 
</p>
<p>The spike nozzle is truncated to 5,175 percent length of a 15 degree 
</p>
<p>conical nozzle of the same area ratio. TI1is results in a nozzle length 
</p>
<p>of about 93 inches along the centerbody axis from the combustor throat, 
</p>
<p>Fig ,17 The nozzle 
</p>
<p>stainless steel tubes 
</p>
<p>attach point requires 
</p>
<p>will be cooled with a tubular wall of about 50 
. 2 per segment. A heat flux of 10 Dtu/in -sec at tfle 
</p>
<p>. 2 
a coolant mass velocity of 4,0 lb/in -sec with a 
</p>
<p>·:1. }.

<p>0.015 inch tube wall thickness. This muy be nchievcd with a 0,20 inch 
</p>
<p>inside tube diameter. The heat flux at the nozzle exit plane is about 
2 2 
</p>
<p>0,9 Btu/in -sec requiring a coolant mass velocity of 0,5 lb/in -sec. 
</p>
<p>The tube width at the exit is 0.150 inches requiring a flat length of 
</p>
<p>about 0.9 inches to achieve the 0,5 mass velocity, 
</p>
<p>Proper design would retain an L/D ratio of about 3 rest1lting in a flat 
</p>
<p>length of about 0,4 inches, This effects a substantial reduction in tube 
</p>
<p>wall weight and simplifies fabrication .. The result is usually a small 
</p>
<p>increase ih coolant pressure drop since the over-cooled wall is irt a low 
</p>
<p>heat flux region near the spike exit. 
</p>
<p>The SERV combustor is very similar to the linear engine cast NARloy segment 
</p>
<p>recently designed and tested under NASA contract NAS8-30182, The operating 
</p>
<p>conditions for the cast segment are similar to those for the SEIW combustor 
</p>
<p>as shown in Table 3 •. The SERV combustor heat load may be predicted from 
</p>
<p>the experimental data taken on the linear engine cast segment, The com­
</p>
<p>posite heat loads to an area ratio of 3.87 1or the foui 11.25 inch side 
</p>
<p>panels are plotted versus chamber pressure in Fig:18 Extrapolating this 
</p>
<p>data to 2000 psia and summing the result yields a total combustor heat load 
</p>
<p>of 630 Btu/sec per inch of _combustor width. 
</p>
<p>A throat mean diameter for the SERV engine of 1026.5 inches yields a total 
6 
</p>
<p>heat load of 2,03 x 10 Btu/sec to an area ratio of 3,87. The heat load for 
</p>
<p>the balance of the SERV shroud is derived from a boundary layer analysis of 
</p>
<p>the contour from E = 3,87 to the ex,i.t at E. = 5,53. This resulted in an 
</p>
<p>additional 112,530 Btu/sec per side, assuming the inner and outer bodies are 
</p>
<p>identical to the shroud exit, A theoretical analysis of the spike nozzle 
</p>
<p>surface indicates an additional contribution of 99],,000 Btu/sec. The total 
-6 engine heat load to be absorbed by fuel coolant is then 3.25 x 10 Btu/sec. .,. 
</p>
<p>If the entire fuel flow is available to cool the thrust chamber walls, a 
</p>
<p>bulk temperature rise of 430 degrees Fis predicted. "Film coefficients 
</p>
<p>for SERV are shown in Figures 19 and 20."

<p>POU~T DESIGN ENGINE PERFORMANCE 
</p>
<p>The SERV vehicle aerospike_ nozzle engine is tailored in diameter (nnd in 
</p>
<p>length) to the base. of .the vehicle •. , This provides a large diameter engine 
</p>
<p>and hence, a high area ratio. The SERV point design engine resulted in a 
</p>
<p>nozzle area ratio of 433,? rind a nozzle percent length of 5.18 percent. 
</p>
<p>ENGINE PERFORMANCE 
</p>
<p>The complete description of the SERV point design, engine .balance, and 
</p>
<p>component efficiency parameters is shown in Table 4 . This information 
</p>
<p>is shown for an engine with an overall throttling capability of 6,53:1. 
</p>
<p>In this table, values are furnished for the various proc~ss efficiencies 
</p>
<p>whose combined effect determine the engine specific impulse. System 
</p>
<p>geometry and flowrates as·we~l as temperature and pressure schedules are 
</p>
<p>presented. 
</p>

</p>
<p>provided together with additional descriptive information on the engine 
</p>
<p>performance calculations,

<p>NOZZLE OPTIMUM THRUST COEFFICIENT RATIO (CF ) 
OPT. 
</p>
<p>At a given altitude, the maximum thrust coefficient occurs when the nozzle 
</p>
<p>exit pressure equals the prevailing ambient pressure, A nozzle whose area 
</p>
<p>ratio can be adjusted at each altitude to match the ambient pressure, will 
</p>
<p>generate an optimum thrust coefficient. The thrust coefficient of this 
</p>
<p>ideal nozzle is obtained using the propellant combination and temperature, 
</p>
<p>mixture ratio, and ch~mber p~essure, and is bjsed on a shifting equilibrium, 
</p>
<p>ideal expansion to the ambient pressure, It is used as a reference for 
</p>
<p>nozzle thrust coefficient efficiency, CT. 
</p>

<p>NOZZLE KINETIC LOSSES, fv( K 
</p>
<p>In chemical equilibrium nozzle flow the various species undergo continuous 
</p>
<p>reactions ns the flow expands in the nozzle~ The reactions are considered 
</p>
<p>to be in chemical equilibrium when they are able to proceed at a faster 
</p>
<p>rate than that imposed by the noizle rate of expansion. When these two 
</p>
<p>rates are equ~l, the co~position of the gas flow remains constant .. The 
</p>
<p>freezing process occurs in e~ch streamline, so that the overall nozzle flow 
</p>
<p>will consist of an upstream region where the species will b~ in chemical 
</p>
<p>equilibrium and a downstream region where the flow is considered frozen. 
</p>
<p>The larger the region of equilibrium flow the higher the performance of 
</p>
<p>the nozzle. 
</p>
<p>The calculation of reaction kinetic effects in the nozzle is performed by 
</p>
<p>dividing th_e nozzle flow into a large number of streamtubes derived from 
</p>
<p>the aerodynamic analysis. The one-dimensional reaction Jdnetic analysis 
</p>
<p>is ·then applied to the flow in each streamtube, The .reaction kinetic loss 
</p>
<p>for the nozzle is calculated by integrating the impulse function across 
</p>
<p>the streamtubes at the nozzle exit for both equilibrium flow and for flow 
</p>
<p>calculat_ed using the kinetic model. For O2/H2 propellants at high thrusts 
</p>
<p>and high chamber pressures the reaction kinetic effects are very small. 
</p>

<p>REGENERATIVE COOLING GAIN 
</p>
<p>Heat gained by the hydrogen during the regenerative cooling of the thrust 
</p>
<p>chamber increases its temperature, Therefore upon injection into the 
</p>
<p>combustion chamber a greater amount of energy results than would be generated 
</p>
<p>by the hydrogen at tank conditions. To properly incorporate this effect a 
</p>
<p>correction is made to the heat of formation of hydrogen from which the ideal 
</p>
<p>specific impulse is calculated at the mixture ratio of the combustion chamber,

<p>APPENDIX A 
</p>
<p>CAS'f SEGMENT EVALUATION 
FINAL REPORT 
</p>
<p>February 1971 
</p>
<p>Contract No. NASS-30182 
</p>
<p>SUMMARY 
</p>
<p>The Cast Segment Evaluation Program has successfully met the objective of 
</p>
<p>establishing the feasib_ility of segmented thrust chamber fabrication using 
</p>
<p>castings for low cost and light weight •. Four segments were built using the 
</p>
<p>simplified procedure, with successive improvements. One segment underwent a 
</p>
<p>series of 110 hot-firing tests and successfully demonstrated design suitability, 
</p>
<p>good performance, and long life. Three segments were assembled together into 
</p>
<p>a linear multisegment and will be test fired under the continuing multisegment 
</p>
<p>effort of contract NASS-25068. In addition, the technology developed has been 
</p>
<p>successfully transferred.to a separate and expanded program to demonstrate a 
</p>
<p>20-segment thrust chamber using the basic segment design.* 
</p>
<p>The cast segment design depended on the development of the thin-walled liner 
</p>
<p>casting of the high (thermal) conductivity alloy designated as NARloy, a North 
</p>
<p>American Rockwell trademark (Fig. 1). In developing this investment casting, 
</p>
<p>the state of the art was extended _in the casting size, complexity,, and the 
</p>
<p>ability to provide thin sections and narrow, deep cooling channels. The casting 
</p>
<p>development efforts included trial castings at two vendors, tooling fabr{cation 
</p>
<p>and a total of 30 experimental castings made under various conditions by the 
</p>
<p>*Breadboard Test Bed Engine, NAS8-25156 
</p>
<p>. E-74 
</p>

<p>selected vendor, Hitchiner Mnnufncturing Company. Problems were encountered and 
</p>
<p>solved in casting areas of shell strength, shell dewaxing, wax cracks, and c;lcn 
</p>
<p>cleanup procedure. Six acceptable castings were made under this technology 
</p>
<p>program. The casting process was developed so that larger orders were 
</p>
<p>success folly filled under a subsequent program. ~'r . 
</p>
<p>The relatively inexpensive cast liner was the basis of the tow-cost segment 
</p>
<p>design. Other design innovations included the extensive use of electroformed 
</p>
<p>nickel to close out the coolant passages and to form manifold joints, The 
. ' 
</p>
<p>segment design was a 100-percent welded or brazed assembly with no joints or 
</p>
<p>seals. During the course of fabrication of the four segments, the l_earning 
</p>
<p>(together with design simplification) resulted in reduced time and cost. Actual 
</p>
<p>-segment weight was 92 pounds, with design proviirion included for further 
</p>
<p>1·eduction t.o · flight weight. 
</p>
<p>A development problem was uncovered when it was found that electroformed 
</p>
<p>nickel is subject to environmental hydrogen embrittlement. The cast segments 
</p>
<p>were strengthened to function with this material, and work was undertaken to 
</p>
<p>provide a complete sol.ution. This work is continuing under other related 
</p>
<p>programs. 
</p>
<p>The tubular nozzle extension for each segment was made as an inexpensive 
</p>
<p>braze assembly of plain, round nickel tubes, brazed flat and formed to contour 
</p>
<p>on simple tooling. ..

<p>The hot-fire test program exceeded expectations in many areas. Performance of 
</p>
<p>the relatively inexpensive injector and small combustion chamber was good; 
</p>
<p>averaged 96,8 percent, and n ,, averaged.97.4 percent, Durability was c,, . 
</p>
<p>n 
Is 
</p>
<p>excellent; 110 hot-firing tests were accomplished on one segment assembly; . some 
</p>
<p>at more severe conditions than normal. Al though fatigue cracks eventually 
</p>
<p>developed in the NARloy liner, perfonnance was not affected and the segment was 
</p>
<p>still suitable for use when retired for examination, Following the test series, 
</p>
<p>the chamber was thoroughly examined and found to fulfill the design intent in 
</p>
<p>all respects,. 
</p>
<p>The segments were stable in mainstage with regard to both acoustic vibration 
</p>
<p>modes and feed system-coupled oscillations. Characteristic vibrations during 
</p>
<p>start were self-damping under all conditions, including tests designed. to 
</p>
<p>explore the low chamber pressure/mixture ratio region. 
</p>
<p>With the satisfactory development of the technology for this particular useful 
</p>
<p>segment size, additional technology effort should be undertaken to extend the 
</p>
<p>range of chamber pressure (higher P) and to provide approaches for ignition 
. C 
</p>
<p>improvement and thrust vector control, Further development of the geometry of 
</p>
<p>miltisegment shapes, such as for linear thrust chamber assemblies with 
</p>
<p>rounded ends, is an important technical challenge, and would include the 
</p>
<p>.. 
optimization and parametric study of chord length, combustion chamber length, 
</p>
<p>thrust/inch, and all aspects of throttling. This continuation of the technology 
</p>
<p>program is recommended to provide the engineering basis for new or enlarged 
</p>
<p>future engine programs,
